HMGB1, a nuclear protein, is released by necrotic and dying cells, and that HMGB1 released by necrotics cells or actively secreted by activated leukocytes, is a trigger of inflammation and of repair programs.

1) HMGB1 is a nuclear protein released by dying cells that is a trigger of inflammation and a signal for tissue repair; 2) DCs secrete high levels of HMGB1 after activation and this secretion is critical for the development of adaptive immune responses.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how the release of HMGB1 by dying cells, and by activated leukocytes, promotes inflammation, tissue repair and autoimmunity.
how the immune system is triggered by tissue injury and how this response can become self-directed.
the role of HMGB1 in innate immunity and its cross-talk with adaptive immunity.

HMGB1 is a master regulator of innate immunity, and a major player in adaptive immunity.

HMGB1 is a master switch of inflammation, a key player in the transition between innate and adaptive immune responses and a potential target for therapy in autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HMGB1 is an important mediator of innate and adaptive immunity.
HMGB1 is a key molecule in the cross-talk between innate and adaptive immune responses.
HMGB1 acts as an alarm signal for innate immunity and as a trigger for adaptive immunity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HMGB1 is an important player at the crossroads of innate and adaptive immunity, and it is a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.
HMGB1 is a key player in the cross-talk between innate and adaptive immune responses, which can be beneficial in the context of infections but may be detrimental in the context of autoimmunity.
